title: Boss: trees
summary: Validate a BST, find a common ancestor, look at a tree from the side, and merge sorted lists with a heap.

steps.title: The tree toolkit
body: Every challenge below uses this class, which the tests provide:
public TreeNode(int value, TreeNode? left = null, TreeNode? right = null)
Reach for recursion when the answer for a node depends on its subtrees, a queue when the question is about rows, and a heap when you keep needing "the smallest so far".

steps.title: Is it a BST?
prompt: Write `bool IsValidBst(TreeNode? root)`: `true` if **every** node is greater than everything in its left subtree and smaller than everything in its right subtree (no duplicates allowed).
Checking only each node against its own children is not enough:
/ \      6 > 4 locally fine, but 6 sits in 5's left subtree:
Pass down the allowed range instead: a helper `Check(node, long min, long max)` where every value must be strictly between `min` and `max`. Going left tightens `max`; going right tightens `min`.
solution: bool Check(TreeNode? node, long min, long max)
if (node.Value <= min || node.Value >= max) return false;
return Check(node.Left, min, node.Value) && Check(node.Right, node.Value, max);
template: Dojo.Eq("a valid BST", true, IsValidBst(new TreeNode(8, new TreeNode(3, new TreeNode(1), new TreeNode(6)), new TreeNode(10, null, new TreeNode(14)))));
Dojo.Eq("6 deep in the left subtree of 5", false, IsValidBst(new TreeNode(5, new TreeNode(4, null, new TreeNode(6)), new TreeNode(8))));
Dojo.Eq("a child on the wrong side", false, IsValidBst(new TreeNode(5, new TreeNode(7))));
Dojo.Eq("duplicates are not allowed", false, IsValidBst(new TreeNode(5, new TreeNode(5))));
Dojo.Eq("an empty tree is valid", true, IsValidBst(null));
Dojo.Eq("extreme values", true, IsValidBst(new TreeNode(0, new TreeNode(int.MinValue), new TreeNode(int.MaxValue))));
public TreeNode(int value, TreeNode? left = null, TreeNode? right = null) { Value = value; Left = left; Right = right; }
hints: Use `long` bounds so `int.MinValue` and `int.MaxValue` themselves can be valid values.

steps.title: Lowest common ancestor
prompt: In a BST, the **lowest common ancestor** of two values is the deepest node that has both in its subtree (a node counts as its own ancestor).

Write `int Lca(TreeNode root, int a, int b)`. Both values are in the tree. Use the BST order: start at the root; if both values are smaller go left, if both are bigger go right; otherwise the paths split here, so this node is the answer. `O(height)`, no traversal of the whole tree needed.
starter: int Lca(TreeNode root, int a, int b)
solution: int Lca(TreeNode root, int a, int b)
if (a < node.Value && b < node.Value) node = node.Left!;
else if (a > node.Value && b > node.Value) node = node.Right!;
template: var dojoT = new TreeNode(8, new TreeNode(3, new TreeNode(1), new TreeNode(6, new TreeNode(4), new TreeNode(7))), new TreeNode(10, null, new TreeNode(14)));
Dojo.Eq("Lca(7, 4) is 6 (order does not matter)", 6, Lca(dojoT, 7, 4));
public TreeNode(int value, TreeNode? left = null, TreeNode? right = null) { Value = value; Left = left; Right = right; }
hints: Loop down from the root; you never need to go back up.
The answer is the first node where `a` and `b` are not both on the same side (or one of them equals the node).

steps.title: Right side view
prompt: Stand to the right of a tree and look at it: you see the **last** node of each row. Write `List<int> RightSideView(TreeNode? root)`.
4    (4 is visible: nothing is to its right)
Level order with rows, keeping the last value of each row.
template: Dojo.Eq("the example", new List<int> { 1, 3, 4 }, RightSideView(new TreeNode(1, new TreeNode(2, null, new TreeNode(4)), new TreeNode(3))));
Dojo.Eq("a left-leaning chain is fully visible", new List<int> { 1, 2, 3 }, RightSideView(new TreeNode(1, new TreeNode(2, new TreeNode(3)))));

Dojo.Eq("a full tree shows its right edge", new List<int> { 4, 6, 7 }, RightSideView(new TreeNode(4, new TreeNode(2, new TreeNode(1), new TreeNode(3)), new TreeNode(6, new TreeNode(5), new TreeNode(7)))));
public TreeNode(int value, TreeNode? left = null, TreeNode? right = null) { Value = value; Left = left; Right = right; }
hints: Use the `queue.Count` row trick from the traversals lesson.
Inside a row of `n` nodes, the node with `i == n - 1` is the visible one.

steps.title: Merge k sorted arrays
prompt: Write `int[] MergeK(int[][] arrays)`: every array is sorted ascending; return all their values in one sorted array.

Use a `PriorityQueue<(int Array, int Index), int>` holding the **front** of each array, keyed by its value. Repeatedly dequeue the smallest, append it, and enqueue the next item from the same array. With `k` arrays and `n` values in total, that is `O(n log k)`.
No sorting: the tests merge 100 arrays of 3,000 values each.
starter: var pq = new PriorityQueue<(int Array, int Index), int>();
solution: var pq = new PriorityQueue<(int Array, int Index), int>();
while (pq.TryDequeue(out var at, out var value))
template: Dojo.Eq("some empty arrays", new[] { 7 }, MergeK(new[] { new int[0], new[] { 7 }, new int[0] }));
Dojo.Eq("no arrays", new int[0], MergeK(new int[0][]));
var dojoArrays = Enumerable.Range(0, 100).Select(a => Enumerable.Range(0, 3000).Select(i => i * 100 + a).ToArray()).ToArray();
Dojo.Eq("100 arrays of 3,000: right length", 300_000, dojoMerged.Length);
Dojo.Eq("100 arrays of 3,000: in order", Enumerable.Range(0, 300_000).ToArray(), dojoMerged);
public TreeNode(int value, TreeNode? left = null, TreeNode? right = null) { Value = value; Left = left; Right = right; }
hints: Start by enqueueing `(a, 0)` with priority `arrays[a][0]` for every non-empty array.
`while (pq.TryDequeue(out var at, out var value))`: append `value`, and if `at.Array` has another item at `at.Index + 1`, enqueue it.
